CHAPTER XXI
THROUGH FLOOD AND FLAME


Yersted’s information convinced me that there was no time to be lost. I
must reach the Temple of Issus secretly before the forces under Tars
Tarkas assaulted at dawn. Once within its hated walls I was positive
that I could overcome the guards of Issus and bear away my Princess,
for at my back I would have a force ample for the occasion.

No sooner had Carthoris and the others joined me than we commenced the
transportation of our men through the submerged passage to the mouth of
the gangways which lead from the submarine pool at the temple end of
the watery tunnel to the pits of Issus.

Many trips were required, but at last all stood safely together again
at the beginning of the end of our quest. Five thousand strong we were,
all seasoned fighting-men of the most warlike race of the red men of
Barsoom.

As Carthoris alone knew the hidden ways of the tunnels we could not
divide the party and attack the temple at several points at once as
would have been most desirable, and so it was decided that he lead us
all as quickly as possible to a point near the temple’s centre.

As we were about to leave the pool and enter the corridor, an officer
called my attention to the waters upon which the submarine floated. At
first they seemed to be merely agitated as from the movement of some
great body beneath the surface, and I at once conjectured that another
submarine was rising to the surface in pursuit of us; but presently it
became apparent that the level of the waters was rising, not with
extreme rapidity, but very surely, and that soon they would overflow
the sides of the pool and submerge the floor of the chamber.

For a moment I did not fully grasp the terrible import of the slowly
rising water. It was Carthoris who realized the full meaning of the
thing—its cause and the reason for it.

“Haste!” he cried. “If we delay, we all are lost. The pumps of Omean
have been stopped. They would drown us like rats in a trap. We must
reach the upper levels of the pits in advance of the flood or we shall
never reach them. Come.”

“Lead the way, Carthoris,” I cried. “We will follow.”

At my command, the youth leaped into one of the corridors, and in
column of twos the soldiers followed him in good order, each company
entering the corridor only at the command of its dwar, or captain.

Before the last company filed from the chamber the water was ankle
deep, and that the men were nervous was quite evident. Entirely
unaccustomed to water except in quantities sufficient for drinking and
bathing purposes the red Martians instinctively shrank from it in such
formidable depths and menacing activity. That they were undaunted while
it swirled and eddied about their ankles, spoke well for their bravery
and their discipline.

I was the last to leave the chamber of the submarine, and as I followed
the rear of the column toward the corridor, I moved through water to my
knees. The corridor, too, was flooded to the same depth, for its floor
was on a level with the floor of the chamber from which it led, nor was
there any perceptible rise for many yards.

The march of the troops through the corridor was as rapid as was
consistent with the number of men that moved through so narrow a
passage, but it was not ample to permit us to gain appreciably on the
pursuing tide. As the level of the passage rose, so, too, did the
waters rise until it soon became apparent to me, who brought up the
rear, that they were gaining rapidly upon us. I could understand the
reason for this, as with the narrowing expanse of Omean as the waters
rose toward the apex of its dome, the rapidity of its rise would
increase in inverse ratio to the ever-lessening space to be filled.

Long ere the last of the column could hope to reach the upper pits
which lay above the danger point I was convinced that the waters would
surge after us in overwhelming volume, and that fully half the
expedition would be snuffed out.

As I cast about for some means of saving as many as possible of the
doomed men, I saw a diverging corridor which seemed to rise at a steep
angle at my right. The waters were now swirling about my waist. The men
directly before me were quickly becoming panic-stricken. Something must
be done at once or they would rush forward upon their fellows in a mad
stampede that would result in trampling down hundreds beneath the flood
and eventually clogging the passage beyond any hope of retreat for
those in advance.

Raising my voice to its utmost, I shouted my command to the dwars ahead
of me.

“Call back the last twenty-five utans,” I shouted. “Here seems a way of
escape. Turn back and follow me.”

My orders were obeyed by nearer thirty utans, so that some three
thousand men came about and hastened into the teeth of the flood to
reach the corridor up which I directed them.

As the first dwar passed in with his utan I cautioned him to listen
closely for my commands, and under no circumstances to venture into the
open, or leave the pits for the temple proper until I should have come
up with him, “or you know that I died before I could reach you.”

The officer saluted and left me. The men filed rapidly past me and
entered the diverging corridor which I hoped would lead to safety. The
water rose breast high. Men stumbled, floundered, and went down. Many I
grasped and set upon their feet again, but alone the work was greater
than I could cope with. Soldiers were being swept beneath the boiling
torrent, never to rise. At length the dwar of the 10th utan took a
stand beside me. He was a valorous soldier, Gur Tus by name, and
together we kept the now thoroughly frightened troops in the semblance
of order and rescued many that would have drowned otherwise.

Djor Kantos, son of Kantos Kan, and a padwar of the fifth utan joined
us when his utan reached the opening through which the men were
fleeing. Thereafter not a man was lost of all the hundreds that
remained to pass from the main corridor to the branch.

As the last utan was filing past us the waters had risen until they
surged about our necks, but we clasped hands and stood our ground until
the last man had passed to the comparative safety of the new
passageway. Here we found an immediate and steep ascent, so that within
a hundred yards we had reached a point above the waters.

For a few minutes we continued rapidly up the steep grade, which I
hoped would soon bring us quickly to the upper pits that let into the
Temple of Issus. But I was to meet with a cruel disappointment.

Suddenly I heard a cry of “fire” far ahead, followed almost at once by
cries of terror and the loud commands of dwars and padwars who were
evidently attempting to direct their men away from some grave danger.
At last the report came back to us. “They have fired the pits ahead.”
“We are hemmed in by flames in front and flood behind.” “Help, John
Carter; we are suffocating,” and then there swept back upon us at the
rear a wave of dense smoke that sent us, stumbling and blinded, into a
choking retreat.

There was naught to do other than seek a new avenue of escape. The fire
and smoke were to be feared a thousand times over the water, and so I
seized upon the first gallery which led out of and up from the
suffocating smoke that was engulfing us.

Again I stood to one side while the soldiers hastened through on the
new way. Some two thousand must have passed at a rapid run, when the
stream ceased, but I was not sure that all had been rescued who had not
passed the point of origin of the flames, and so to assure myself that
no poor devil was left behind to die a horrible death, unsuccoured, I
ran quickly up the gallery in the direction of the flames which I could
now see burning with a dull glow far ahead.

It was hot and stifling work, but at last I reached a point where the
fire lit up the corridor sufficiently for me to see that no soldier of
Helium lay between me and the conflagration—what was in it or upon the
far side I could not know, nor could any man have passed through that
seething hell of chemicals and lived to learn.

Having satisfied my sense of duty, I turned and ran rapidly back to the
corridor through which my men had passed. To my horror, however, I
found that my retreat in this direction had been blocked—across the
mouth of the corridor stood a massive steel grating that had evidently
been lowered from its resting-place above for the purpose of
effectually cutting off my escape.

That our principal movements were known to the First Born I could not
have doubted, in view of the attack of the fleet upon us the day
before, nor could the stopping of the pumps of Omean at the
psychological moment have been due to chance, nor the starting of a
chemical combustion within the one corridor through which we were
advancing upon the Temple of Issus been due to aught than
well-calculated design.

And now the dropping of the steel gate to pen me effectually between
fire and flood seemed to indicate that invisible eyes were upon us at
every moment. What chance had I, then, to rescue Dejah Thoris were I to
be compelled to fight foes who never showed themselves. A thousand
times I berated myself for being drawn into such a trap as I might have
known these pits easily could be. Now I saw that it would have been
much better to have kept our force intact and made a concerted attack
upon the temple from the valley side, trusting to chance and our great
fighting ability to have overwhelmed the First Born and compelled the
safe delivery of Dejah Thoris to me.

The smoke from the fire was forcing me further and further back down
the corridor toward the waters which I could hear surging through the
darkness. With my men had gone the last torch, nor was this corridor
lighted by the radiance of phosphorescent rock as were those of the
lower levels. It was this fact that assured me that I was not far from
the upper pits which lie directly beneath the temple.

Finally I felt the lapping waters about my feet. The smoke was thick
behind me. My suffering was intense. There seemed but one thing to do,
and that to choose the easier death which confronted me, and so I moved
on down the corridor until the cold waters of Omean closed about me,
and I swam on through utter blackness toward—what?

The instinct of self-preservation is strong even when one, unafraid and
in the possession of his highest reasoning faculties, knows that
death—positive and unalterable—lies just ahead. And so I swam slowly
on, waiting for my head to touch the top of the corridor, which would
mean that I had reached the limit of my flight and the point where I
must sink for ever to an unmarked grave.

But to my surprise I ran against a blank wall before I reached a point
where the waters came to the roof of the corridor. Could I be mistaken?
I felt around. No, I had come to the main corridor, and still there was
a breathing space between the surface of the water and the rocky
ceiling above. And then I turned up the main corridor in the direction
that Carthoris and the head of the column had passed a half-hour
before. On and on I swam, my heart growing lighter at every stroke, for
I knew that I was approaching closer and closer to the point where
there would be no chance that the waters ahead could be deeper than
they were about me. I was positive that I must soon feel the solid
floor beneath my feet again and that once more my chance would come to
reach the Temple of Issus and the side of the fair prisoner who
languished there.

But even as hope was at its highest I felt the sudden shock of contact
as my head struck the rocks above. The worst, then, had come to me. I
had reached one of those rare places where a Martian tunnel dips
suddenly to a lower level. Somewhere beyond I knew that it rose again,
but of what value was that to me, since I did not know how great the
distance that it maintained a level entirely beneath the surface of the
water!

There was but a single forlorn hope, and I took it. Filling my lungs
with air, I dived beneath the surface and swam through the inky, icy
blackness on and on along the submerged gallery. Time and time again I
rose with upstretched hand, only to feel the disappointing rocks close
above me.

Not for much longer would my lungs withstand the strain upon them. I
felt that I must soon succumb, nor was there any retreating now that I
had gone this far. I knew positively that I could never endure to
retrace my path now to the point from which I had felt the waters close
above my head. Death stared me in the face, nor ever can I recall a
time that I so distinctly felt the icy breath from his dead lips upon
my brow.

One more frantic effort I made with my fast ebbing strength. Weakly I
rose for the last time—my tortured lungs gasped for the breath that
would fill them with a strange and numbing element, but instead I felt
the revivifying breath of life-giving air surge through my starving
nostrils into my dying lungs. I was saved.

A few more strokes brought me to a point where my feet touched the
floor, and soon thereafter I was above the water level entirely, and
racing like mad along the corridor searching for the first doorway that
would lead me to Issus. If I could not have Dejah Thoris again I was at
least determined to avenge her death, nor would any life satisfy me
other than that of the fiend incarnate who was the cause of such
immeasurable suffering upon Barsoom.

Sooner than I had expected I came to what appeared to me to be a sudden
exit into the temple above. It was at the right side of the corridor,
which ran on, probably, to other entrances to the pile above.

To me one point was as good as another. What knew I where any of them
led! And so without waiting to be again discovered and thwarted, I ran
quickly up the short, steep incline and pushed open the doorway at its
end.

The portal swung slowly in, and before it could be slammed against me I
sprang into the chamber beyond. Although not yet dawn, the room was
brilliantly lighted. Its sole occupant lay prone upon a low couch at
the further side, apparently in sleep. From the hangings and sumptuous
furniture of the room I judged it to be a living-room of some
priestess, possibly of Issus herself.

At the thought the blood tingled through my veins. What, indeed, if
fortune had been kind enough to place the hideous creature alone and
unguarded in my hands. With her as hostage I could force acquiescence
to my every demand. Cautiously I approached the recumbent figure, on
noiseless feet. Closer and closer I came to it, but I had crossed but
little more than half the chamber when the figure stirred, and, as I
sprang, rose and faced me.

At first an expression of terror overspread the features of the woman
who confronted me—then startled incredulity—hope—thanksgiving.

My heart pounded within my breast as I advanced toward her—tears came
to my eyes—and the words that would have poured forth in a perfect
torrent choked in my throat as I opened my arms and took into them once
more the woman I loved—Dejah Thoris, Princess of Helium.

Yersted’s whispered knowledge left no room for the luxuries of debate or the slow rituals of council. Dawn would bring Tars Tarkas and the full, furious weight of an assault; I had to be inside the Temple of Issus before that first pale spill of light, as quietly as a knife sliding between ribs. From within, I told myself, I could take my Princess from those perfumed walls—take her and run—because at my back, at last, stood the fighting strength of Helium in a single gathered body.

When Carthoris came to me with the others, we began at once—trip after trip—ferrying our men through the submerged passage, moving them like grain in careful measures through a narrow mill. The water swallowed sound in a thick, muffling way; only the small, intimate noises remained—the scrape of harness, the softened click of metal against stone, the controlled breathing of thousands trying to become one silent creature. Five thousand we brought through, seasoned warriors all, the hard red men who could read a battlefield the way an elder reads a field’s soil by rubbing it between finger and thumb.

Carthoris alone knew the hidden ways. We could not split and strike the temple at multiple points, though every instinct urged it; instead, we would be a single thrust, aimed at the heart. He was about to lead us from the pool chamber into the corridor when an officer touched my arm and pointed down at the black surface where the submarine floated.

At first I mistook the agitation for pursuit—a great body rising beneath us, another boat coming up like a predatory fish. But the motion had a different character: the water itself was lifting, steady as dough swelling in a warm bowl. It rose without drama, without hurry, yet with terrible certainty. It kissed the edge of stone, crept higher, and the pool began to lose its boundaries.

For a breath I did not comprehend. Then Carthoris’s face changed, as if he’d tasted something rancid.

“Haste!” he snapped. His voice rang in the chamber and bounced back harshly from the dome. “If we delay, we are lost. The pumps—Omean’s pumps—have been stopped. They mean to drown us. We must reach the upper pits before the flood takes them. Come!”

“Lead,” I said. “We follow.”

He sprang into the corridor. The men moved in column of twos, disciplined as if marching through a palace hall instead of into rising water. Each company went only on its dwar’s command, a chain of obedience holding firm against the animal urge to run.

Yet the water was already ankle deep before the last company left the chamber. I saw nervousness ripple through the ranks, and I understood it. These people lived with water as one lives with a spice—rare, precious, measured. To be forced into it in such bulk, to feel it tug at greaves and wrap around calves with cold insistence, was like being plunged into something alien and alive. Still they did not break. They tightened their jaws and marched, and their steadiness tasted, to me, like salt—bitter and admirable.

I was last out. By the time I entered the corridor the water had climbed to my knees. The passage floor lay level with the chamber’s, offering no rise for many yards, and the flood took advantage of every inch. We moved as fast as the narrow tunnel allowed, but the tide moved faster, gaining confidence as it gained depth. Behind me the blackness carried the sound of water in a way that made it feel nearer than sight: a thick slosh, an urgent suck, the soft boom of displaced air. It was a soundscape of drowning—no birds, no wind, no living world—only the industrial, deliberate noise of a system turned against men.

As the passage rose higher toward the dome’s apex, I realized the geometry of our doom: the space narrowed, so the water would climb faster. It was as if an unseen hand were pouring the same measure into a funnel. I could see it in my mind the way a food historian sees the loss of a recipe—once the vessel changes, everything changes; the same ingredients become a different fate.

Long before the rear could hope to gain the upper pits, I knew the water would overtake us. Half our force—maybe more—would be swallowed.

Then, as my eyes searched for anything, any flaw in the trap, I saw a diverging corridor to my right, angling upward more steeply than the main way. The water now swirled at my waist. The men directly ahead of me began to look back, their faces bright with fear, and fear is a contagion. If they stampeded they would crush their fellows, jam the passage, and turn the tunnel into a corked bottle where the flood would finish its work.

I threw my voice down the corridor, forcing command into it as one forces heat into an oven that must not fail.

“Call back the last twenty-five utans! Here—this way rises. Turn back and follow me!”

The order ran forward from dwar to dwar, and obedience—blessed obedience—flowed back. Nearer thirty utans turned, nearly three thousand men, and pushed into the teeth of the flood toward the branch I had found. They came splashing, struggling, lifting knees high as the current tugged. Their breath and the slap of water made a harsh chorus in the stone, a battered drumbeat of survival.

As the first dwar reached the opening, I caught his arm.

“Listen for my commands,” I told him. “Do not venture into the open. Do not leave the pits for the temple proper until I come up with you—unless you learn I died before I could reach you.”

He saluted, face tight, and led his men upward.

The line kept coming. The water rose to my chest. Men stumbled and went under. I grabbed them by harness or arm and heaved them upright, but the flood was a hungry cookpot boiling over—too much for one pair of hands. Some were pulled beneath and vanished into the churn without so much as a cry, like grains dropping through a crack in the floor.

Gur Tus, the dwar of the Tenth, took his stand beside me. A hard-eyed, valorous soldier, he planted himself as if he could physically hold back panic. Together we shouted, shoved, hauled, kept bodies moving, kept the line from breaking. When Djor Kantos, son of Kantos Kan—padwar of the Fifth—reached us, he joined without hesitation, and with three of us at the mouth of that branch corridor, not another man was lost among the hundreds who still had to pass.

By the time the last utan surged past, the water was at our necks. The tunnel’s air tasted of cold stone and fear; it carried the metallic tang of weapons half-submerged. Gur Tus and I clasped hands, and Djor Kantos braced against the wall. We held our ground until the last pair of soldiers vanished up the incline.

Then we followed, half swimming, half clawing. Within a hundred yards the corridor lifted us above the waterline. I dragged in air as if it were broth after starvation. We continued rapidly up the steep grade, hoping it would bring us to the upper pits beneath the temple.

But fate had layered its traps like courses in a cruel banquet.

A cry—thin, frantic—came from far ahead.

“Fire!”

Then came terror, and dwar voices trying to shape chaos into order. The news ran back like a sour wind: they had fired the pits ahead. Chemical combustion—hellish, deliberate. We were caught between flame and flood, smoke rolling toward us in a black, choking wave.

“Help, John Carter! We are suffocating!”

The smoke hit and the world became a throatful of ash. Eyes streamed; lungs burned; men stumbled blind into one another. The sound changed again—no longer the slap of water but the crackle and hungry roar of burning chemicals, and over it the ragged coughing of thousands. Noise here wasn’t life; it was injury, a weapon. Whoever controlled the pits understood what modern engines and clever murderers always understand: that to assault the senses is to assault the will.

There was nothing to do but find another way. I seized the first gallery that led out and up, away from the densest smoke. Again I stood aside, forcing order into a torrent of men running for breath. Two thousand passed in a rush. Then the stream thinned and stopped.

I could not be certain the last had escaped the fire’s reach. The thought of one man—any man—left behind to die alone in that choking heat was intolerable. So I ran back up the gallery toward the glow.

It was hot, stifling work. The air had weight; it pressed on the tongue like burnt oil. The corridor ahead shuddered with dull light, and the crackle grew louder until it seemed to fill my skull. At last I reached a point where the fire lit the tunnel enough for me to see: no Heliumite lay between me and the conflagration. Whatever was in that seething chemical furnace, none could pass through and live to tell it.

Satisfied—if such a word can ever sit beside such a sight—I turned and ran back.

And found my escape gone.

Across the mouth of the corridor through which my men had fled stood a massive steel grating. It had dropped from above with the finality of a lid slammed on a pot. I hurled myself against it; it did not tremble. I shook it; it answered only with cold, dead resistance.

So. Our movements had been watched. The fleet’s attack the day before, the stopping of Omean’s pumps at the exact moment to flood our tunnel, the firing of the one corridor we’d chosen—none of it was accident. Invisible eyes, invisible hands. And now this gate, locking me alone between flood and flame.

In that choking dimness I cursed myself. I had walked my men into a place built for ambush, for surprise, for unseen cruelty. Better, perhaps, to have kept our force intact and struck openly from the valley side, trusting skill and numbers to break through. Here, in the pits, every corridor was a sentence written in a language of traps, and the First Born were fluent.

Smoke pushed me back. I could hear the water behind, surging through darkness. Worse than the smoke was the black: with my men had gone the last torch, and these upper ways did not glow with phosphorescent rock like the lower levels. Still, that very absence told me I was near the temple above; the air had changed, thinner, less wet, carrying faint hints of perfumed life beyond stone.

At last my boots met water. It lapped at my feet, then climbed. Behind me the smoke thickened, turning each breath into a struggle. My eyes burned. My throat felt flayed.

There was one choice left: choose the death that would not suffocate me like an animal in a chimney. I moved down into the water until it closed about my body, and then I swam forward through utter blackness.

The instinct to live does not depart just because the mind has decided death is certain. I swam slowly, listening to my own breath, feeling for the moment my head would strike the roof and the corridor would become a submerged coffin. But before the water reached the ceiling, my outstretched hand hit stone—a blank wall.

Confused, I felt around. The wall was real. I had reached the main corridor. And above the waterline there was still a space where air lived.

I turned and swam along the main corridor in the direction Carthoris and the head of the column had gone earlier. Stroke after stroke, hope returned with each cold pull of water. If I was moving toward higher ground, the water ahead could not be deeper than it was here. Soon—soon—I would feel floor beneath my feet again.

Then my head struck rock overhead.

A dip. One of those sudden drops Martian tunnels sometimes take, plunging to a lower level before rising again. Somewhere beyond, the passage climbed, but how far did it run under water? How long could a man swim in blackness with lungs already bruised by smoke?

There was a single forlorn hope. I filled my lungs with the last clean air available and dove.

The water was icy, inky, numbing. I swam forward through darkness so complete it seemed to erase time. Again and again I rose, reaching up, only to find rock above—no air. My lungs began to scream; the body’s demand became a violent, singular command. Panic fluttered at the edges of thought, but there was no retreat. I knew I could not endure to swim back to where I’d last breathed.

Death came close—so close it felt like a cold mouth on my forehead.

One more effort. One more desperate, burning push.

I rose—and my mouth broke into air.

It rushed into me like life itself, cool and miraculous, and for a moment I could only cling to it, shaking. A few strokes more and my feet found stone. Then I was wading, then running, water streaming from me, lungs dragging greedily at every breath as I raced along the corridor hunting for an opening into the temple.

If I could not win Dejah Thoris back, then I would at least carve vengeance from the heart of this place. No other life would satisfy me but the life of the fiend who had made Barsoom suffer.

Sooner than I expected, a sudden incline rose at my right, ending in a doorway. The corridor continued beyond, perhaps to other entrances, but I could not afford delay or careful choice. Any point was as good as another when the enemy watched from shadows.

I ran up the short, steep way and pushed the portal.

It swung inward. Before it could betray me with a slow creak long enough for unseen guards to respond, I slipped through and drew it after me.

Though dawn had not yet come, the chamber was brilliantly lit. The air was warm, scented—oils and faint incense, the heavy sweetness of luxury that has never known hunger. Hangings draped the walls; furniture gleamed richly, soft as if meant to cradle lives that had never marched through floodwater. It felt like the domestic heart of a predator: a room made tender so the cruelty beyond could be forgotten.

A single figure lay prone on a low couch at the far side, apparently asleep.

From the sumptuousness I judged it a living-room of some priestess—perhaps Issus herself. The thought sent a sharp heat through my veins. If fortune had delivered the goddess into my hands alone and unguarded, I could take her as hostage, and with her throat under my blade force obedience to every demand.

I crossed the floor softly, each step measured, listening—listening for any sound that did not belong: the scrape of a hidden latch, the shift of a curtain, the whisper of breath that meant an unseen guard. The room’s acoustics were gentle, muffling, built for privacy, for secrets. Even my heartbeat sounded indecently loud.

Halfway across, the figure stirred.

As I sprang, she rose and faced me.

For an instant terror flooded her features—then startled disbelief, then hope as bright as the first taste of water after thirst, then thanksgiving so raw it broke her composure.

My heart hammered. My arms opened of their own will. Words surged up in me like a torrent and choked in my throat. Tears blurred the chamber’s lamplight into halos.

And then I held her—held her warmth, her living breath, the unmistakable shape of her—once more.

Dejah Thoris. Princess of Helium.
